description: We are Students from Universitas Negeri Padang, currently interested in how gravity works, technology, data, and space exploration. We are passionate about learning, building creative solutions, and turning complex scientific ideas into something that is easier and more interesting for everyone to understand.
summary:
Geodesic is a browser game where anyone can become a mission engineer. You build a rocket piece by piece, design a spacecraft, chain gravity-assist flybys across the real solar system, then fly the mission yourself, from the first second of liftoff to the last metre of a landing.

A spacecraft can fall toward a moving planet, swing around it, and leave faster than it arrived, without burning any fuel. Voyager reached the outer planets this way. In Geodesic, players discover it for themselves: one big number shows exactly how much propellant each slingshot saves.

Players balance budget, mass, power, data, communications and time. Teams of 1–4 players can each take a role. An interactive tutorial gets newcomers flying in about 60 seconds, and five missions run from the Moon to Neptune.

Most students only read about orbits and gravity. They never get to try, miss the planet, and understand why. Geodesic turns textbook physics into decisions with consequences, and it runs on real NASA/JPL planetary data. The flight engine reproduces the trajectories of Voyager 1, Voyager 2 and New Horizons to within 3%. All it needs is a browser and curiosity.
details:
What it does

Geodesic walks players through the life of a real mission:

  1. Choose a destination. The Moon (beginner) through Mars, Jupiter and Saturn to Neptune (expert). Each mission teaches one hard lesson: the rocket equation, launch windows, borrowed speed, weak sunlight, extreme distance.
  2. Build the rocket. Tanks, engines, boosters, upper stages and fairings snap together live in 3D. One click explodes the rocket into labelled parts. An X-ray cutaway reveals the tanks, plumbing and engines inside. Every change instantly updates delta-v, thrust-to-weight, mass and cost.
  3. Build the spacecraft. Bus size, solar panels or RTGs, antenna size and science instruments. Power falls with the square of the distance from the Sun, and the data rate falls with distance from Earth, so Saturn needs a very different spacecraft from Mars.
  4. Plan the route. Planets sit where JPL's orbital elements put them on the chosen date. Click planets to chain flybys, slide the launch date to find a window, and watch the propellant saved by each gravity assist update.
  5. Go / No-Go poll. As in real mission control, each console (Propulsion, Power & Comms, Science, Route, Budget) calls GO or NO-GO, explains why, and links straight to the fix.
  6. Fly it as flight director. You start the gravity turn and separate the stages. During cruise you hold to burn course corrections. You aim each flyby's closest approach, then time the capture burn at the moment the engine is most effective. On the Moon and Mars, you land.
  7. Read the report. Propellant used and saved, science returned, cost, a burn timeline, a Physics Breakdown of why the mission succeeded or failed, and a mission patch generated for your flight.

Failure is honest, and it teaches. A rocket that runs out of propellant before reaching orbit falls back and explodes. A spacecraft whose tank runs dry in deep space does not explode; it misses its target or drifts away forever, as real spacecraft do.

How it works

Under the game sits a real astrodynamics engine:

  • Rocket equation (delta-v = Isp x g0 x ln(m0/m1)) for every stage and every burn
  • Vis-viva for departure, capture and periapsis burns, including the Oberth effect
  • Patched conics with hyperbolic flyby geometry
  • A universal-variable Lambert solver to find the arc between two planets in a given time
  • Kepler propagation to fly the spacecraft along its real path
  • A 2-D ascent simulation with an atmosphere, drag, max-Q and staging
  • Planet positions from JPL's Keplerian elements at the exact date

Learning built in

  • Two Minds, One Universe. An interactive 3D lab where players change mass, distance and speed to see Newton's gravity reshape an orbit, then switch to Einstein to see how gravity bends time. It also explains the game's name: in general relativity, a free-falling spacecraft follows the straightest path through curved spacetime, which is called a geodesic.
  • Physics Insights during each flight phase shows the equations at work.
  • Classroom mode. A teacher creates a room code, teams join from their own devices, and a live leaderboard ranks them by Mission Score, Fuel Saver, Most Science, Cheapest Success and Fastest Arrival. A "Best failure lesson" tab recognises that some of the best learning comes from things going wrong.

Benefits

  • No installation, no account, no cost. It runs in any modern browser.
  • It turns abstract formulas into choices with visible consequences.
  • It teaches engineering trade-offs: there is never one perfect answer, only better compromises.
  • It is built for classrooms, with team roles and room codes, so it fits real lessons.
  • It is honest science. Every simplification is labelled as a "game model", and every number can be traced to its source.

What we hope to achieve

We want a student in a small town, with nothing but a laptop and a question, to plan a route across the solar system and see how gravity works. We want them to watch it fail, understand why, try again, and feel the moment when a planet hands them speed for free. We hope Geodesic can grow into a classroom tool for schools across Indonesia and beyond, so that the next generation of mission designers starts by playing.

Tools and languages

  • Languages: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, SQL
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (3D graphics)
  • Backend: Node.js, Express
  • Database: TiDB Cloud Serverless (MySQL-compatible)
  • Testing: Node test runner, Playwright with Google Chrome (end-to-end playthroughs and screenshot comparison)
  • SI tools: Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex
  • Software: Visual Studio Code, Google Chrome, Windows 11
  • Hardware: Advan Workplus AMD Ryzen 5, Acer Nitro 5 AMD Ryzen 7
